Q: Fix Chocolatey "Access is Denied" A:

To those who reach this page searching for a solution. The issue is caused by anti-virus (in my case crowdstrike) that prevented access to the folder. The easiest solution was to use system powershell host instead of inbuilt.

Either permanently set:

choco feature disable -n powershellHost

or run the installation as follows for the affected packages:

choco install --use-system-powershell <pkg>

Q: How to check a `struct gps_data_t*` for a NULL value the safe way? A:

This feels like a cheap workaround for a possibly deeper issue somewhere in either your code or in the library code.

It should be exactly the same as

if ((response = instance -> gps_handler.stream (WATCH_ENABLE | WATCH_JSON)) == nullptr)

In fact, it should create the exact same code.

What does the full call stack really say when you get the crash? What is the last place in your code that it happens?

If you don't fix the deeper issue, it will come back and haunt you when you least expect it.

Q: SCIP CPU usage is low while solving A:

If you used a binary distribution, it might have been already compiled with that setting on; I think it is referred to as "parascip" - I see on the download page some versions say "no parascip", while others don't.

In any case, parallelization is not easy to implement and control, and depending on the problem you're having it's not guaranteed to improve the performance as much as theoretically possible, i.e., 10x from 10% CPU to 100% CPU.

At the same time, if it makes sense to your problem, you might consider a simple parallelization strategy of your own: just launch several versions of the program with different parameters at the same time, as they will not slow down each other if their number is less than the number of performance cores of your CPU.

Q: Link for Informix CSDK 3.70 for 32-bit Windows Server 2003 A:

Since IBM Informix Client SDK 3.70 was released in October 2010, it is unlikely you will be able to find legitimate copies of it. Your best bet is to speak to IBM Informix Technical Support, assuming you have a support contract. Otherwise, it is probably time to upgrade to a more recent version of the client and server — and a 64-bit version of it.

Q: Filtering rows across multiple columns A:

I went through your screenshot and description carefully, and I think I see where the issue is coming from.

Right now you’re applying filters on each column individually (like “> 0”), but Excel treats those filters separately. So if the first column is blank, that row gets hidden—even if other columns in that same row actually have values. That’s why some rows are disappearing when they shouldn’t.

What you really need here is to evaluate the entire row at once, not column-by-column.

Simple way to fix it

Add a helper column (you can call it something like "Has Data") and use this formula:

=COUNT(D2:G2)>0

(Adjust D:G to match your quantity columns)

This basically checks:
**
Does this row have at least one value in any of these columns?**

Then just:

  1. Drag the formula down

  2. Apply a filter on this new column

  3. Select TRUE

Now Excel will keep any row where at least one of those columns has a value, and hide rows where everything is blank.

Why this works better

Instead of filtering each column separately, this approach looks at the row as a whole. So even if one column is blank, the row will still stay visible as long as another column has a value.

This should keep the exact rows you mentioned (like 55, 59, 60, 68) visible after filtering.
